title: Maniabandha: Where Odisha’s Weaving Heritage Meets a New Generation of Travellers
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: In this village in Cuttack district, the future of textile tourism depends on understanding the skill behind the sari—and keeping its makers at the centre.

image.alt: Illustration of dyed yarn, a wooden shuttle and patterned cloth beside a handloom.
image.caption: Editorial illustration inspired by bandha weaving; not a photograph of Maniabandha or a documented textile.

passages.text: A patterned sari begins long before the cloth takes shape. In the weft ikat tradition associated with Maniabandha, the design is planned in yarn: sections are bound, colour is applied, and the prepared threads are woven into a pattern. What a buyer sees as a finished motif begins as a series of decisions about placement, colour and alignment.

That process offers a compelling reason to visit Maniabandha, a weaving village in the Badamba area of Odisha’s Cuttack district. The district’s export action plan describes the village and neighbouring Nuapatna as a region of concentrated weaving activity, working predominantly in cotton, with silk also present. Here, a textile can become an introduction to the people and knowledge behind its making.

The craft is commonly known in Odisha as bandha. Unlike a design printed onto finished fabric, ikat is created by resist-dyeing yarn before weaving. In weft ikat, the pattern is carried by the crosswise threads. The work demands coordination between preparation and weaving: the design must remain intelligible as separate lengths of coloured yarn become cloth. Tata Trusts’ documentation of Maniabandha shows yarn preparation and dyeing as part of a wider household craft economy, drawing attention to work that is easily overlooked when only the finished sari is displayed.

Maniabandha’s cultural setting adds another dimension. Odisha Tourism describes a village shaped by Buddhist and Hindu communities, with textiles featuring motifs such as lotus flowers, elephants and lions. These traditions invite careful interpretation. A motif may carry different meanings for different makers; hearing a weaver explain a design can be more revealing than assigning every pattern a single religious meaning.

The neighbouring weaving centres also belong to the wider story of Khandua textiles and the Jagannath tradition. The Development Commissioner (Handicrafts)’ GI compendium records Nuapatna’s historic connection with cloth woven for the deities at Puri and includes Maniabandha Weavers’ Cooperative Society among the registration holders for Khandua Saree and Fabrics. This connection places the region’s weaving within a continuing relationship between craft and worship.

The names deserve precision. Khandua’s existing GI recognition should not be confused with the separate application for “Maniabandhi Saree.” As checked on 29 October 2026, the latter remained at the examination stage in the official GI registry. Recognising the relationship between these textile traditions need not erase their distinct identities.

Maniabandha’s appeal has received national recognition. It was among the winners in the crafts category of the Ministry of Tourism’s Best Tourism Villages Competition in 2024. Odisha Tourism now presents the village as a destination for watching weaving, meeting makers and purchasing textiles directly. The recognition offers a chance to bring the work of its artisans to a wider audience.

Preparing artisans to welcome visitors has also been part of Odisha’s wider approach. In September 2022, The New Indian Express reported that the Handlooms, Textiles and Handicrafts department had enlisted IITTM faculty for a proposed training programme covering 730 artisans and entrepreneurs across 73 handloom clusters. An initial group of 80 weavers from four districts, including Cuttack, had received hospitality and soft-skills training. This is evidence of a statewide initiative; it does not establish a new or continuing Maniabandha-specific course.

The question of where tourism happens matters to the community. On 6 January 2026, The New Indian Express reported that weavers represented by the Maniabandha Handloom Cluster Consortium opposed locating the proposed Maniabandha Buddhist Handloom Village Tourism Centre in nearby Abhimanpur. They wanted it established in Maniabandha itself. The report also recorded the district collector’s position that the centre would be built in Abhimanpur. The disagreement concerns a proposed facility, and should not be read as evidence that a completed centre is open to visitors.

The issue carries a wider lesson for craft tourism: location influences which households visitors meet, where they spend and whose account of a place they hear. A successful project needs the participation of the people whose work gives it meaning.

There is relevant experience in artisan enterprise. Tata Trusts includes Maniabandha among the clusters supported by Antaran, its craft livelihoods programme. Its approach combines design education, business skills, pricing, communication and connections with buyers. These are practical foundations for tourism too: an engaging demonstration has greater value when the artisan can set its terms, explain the product and retain a fair return.

The craft is also finding new ways to make its provenance visible. In its August 2026 magazine, Tata Trusts describes an Antaran pilot with technology company Kosha across three weaving clusters, including Maniabandha. Loom sensors and QR labels help connect participating textiles to information about their making. The programme’s account also acknowledges practical challenges, from tagging fabric that will later be cut to artisans’ concerns about designs being copied online. The pilot suggests a useful direction: buyers should be able to learn who made a textile and understand what they are paying for.

For travellers, a thoughtful visit begins with an arrangement rather than an expectation that every working household is open to the public. Ask before entering or photographing, agree on any demonstration fee, and allow time for the maker’s explanation. When buying, ask about the fibre, technique, care requirements and who made the piece. Such questions help turn a purchase into an informed appreciation of labour and skill.

For Maniabandha, the most useful measure of tourism will be what it contributes to weaving households: paid time, worthwhile orders, stronger customer relationships and opportunities for younger artisans. A visitor who understands how a pattern takes shape may leave with more than a sari. They may leave knowing whose work they want to support again.
